dhpak2.3:1.1: 2.3 The Story about the Elder Culla Panthaka
dhpak2.3:2.1: “Through activity, heedfulness,” [28.299] {1.239} this Dhamma teaching was given by the
dhpak2.3:2.2: Teacher while he was in residence at Veḷuvana with reference to Culla Panthaka the elder.
dhpak2.3:3.1: We are told that the daughter of a rich merchant of Rājagaha, upon reaching the age of maturity, was guarded by her
dhpak2.3:3.2: mother and father on the topmost floor of a seven-storied palace with excessive care. But in spite of this, maddened
dhpak2.3:3.3: with the madness of youth and lusting for a man, {1.240} she had intercourse with her own slave. Frightened to think
dhpak2.3:3.4: that others also might find out about her misconduct, she said to him: “It is out of the question for us to live here
dhpak2.3:3.5: any longer. If my mother and father discover my misconduct, they will tear me limb from limb. Let us go live elsewhere.”
dhpak2.3:4.1: So taking a few necessary things they could carry in the hand, they left the house by the principal door. “It matters
dhpak2.3:4.2: little,” said they, “where we go, so long as we go and live where others will know nothing about us.” So saying, the
dhpak2.3:4.3: two set out together. They took up their residence in a certain place and lived together, with the result that the
dhpak2.3:4.4: young wife conceived a child in her womb. When her unborn child reached maturity, she took counsel with her husband,
dhpak2.3:4.5: saying: “If I give birth to my child in a place far removed from kith and kin, it will bring suffering to both of us.
dhpak2.3:4.6: There is but one place for us to go, and that is home to my parents.” But her husband, fearing that, if he himself went
dhpak2.3:4.7: there, he would be killed, kept postponing the day of their departure, saying: “We will go today; we will go tomorrow.”
dhpak2.3:5.1: The young wife thought to herself: “This fool realizes the [28.300] enormity of his offense, and therefore dares not
dhpak2.3:5.2: go. After all, a mother and a father wish one only well. Let this fellow go or not; at any rate I intend to go.” So
dhpak2.3:5.3: while her husband was out of the house, she put the household utensils away, and informing her next-door neighbors
dhpak2.3:5.4: that she was going home to her parents, she started out on the road. When her husband returned to the house and failed
dhpak2.3:5.5: to see her, he enquired of the neighbors where she had gone. Hearing that she had gone home to her parents, he set
dhpak2.3:5.6: out after her as fast as he could and overtook her on the road. And right there she gave birth to her child. “What is
dhpak2.3:5.7: it, wife?” asked the husband. {1.241} “Husband, it is a son.” – “What shall we do now?” – “That for which we intended
dhpak2.3:5.8: to go home to my parents has happened by the way. Why, therefore, should we go there? Let us return to our own home.”
dhpak2.3:6.1: Agreeing that this was the best plan, husband and wife returned to their own home. Since their son had been born by the
dhpak2.3:6.2: way, they gave him the name Panthaka (Wayfarer). In no long time the young wife conceived a second child in her womb.
dhpak2.3:6.3: All is to be related in detail precisely as before. Since this child also was born by the way, they gave him the name
dhpak2.3:6.4: Culla Panthaka, calling the older son Mahā Panthaka. Taking their two sons, they returned to their own place of residence.
dhpak2.3:7.1: While they were living there Mahā Panthaka heard other boys speak of their uncles and grandparents. So one day he
dhpak2.3:7.2: asked his mother: “Mother, other boys speak of their grandfather and grandmother. Haven’t we any relatives?” – “Yes,
dhpak2.3:7.3: my son. You have no relatives living here, but you have a grandfather, a rich merchant, living in Rājagaha, and we
dhpak2.3:7.4: have many other relatives living there too.” – “Why don’t we go there, mother?” The mother evaded telling her son
dhpak2.3:7.5: why she did not go there. But the children repeated the question time and again. Finally she said to her husband:
dhpak2.3:7.6: {1.242} “These children weary me excessively. Will my mother and father eat us alive when they see us? Come, why not
dhpak2.3:7.7: let the children see the family of their grandparents?” – “I should not dare meet them face to face, but I will escort
dhpak2.3:7.8: you there.” – “Very well, some means must be found by which the children can see the family of their grandparents.”
dhpak2.3:8.1: So mother and father took the children, and arriving at Rājagaha in due course, took up their residence in the hall of
dhpak2.3:8.2: a certain woman near the gate of the city. Then the mother of the children sent word to her mother and father that she
dhpak2.3:8.3: and her children had arrived. When her parents received this message, they said to each other: “As we have passed
dhpak2.3:8.4: through the round of existences, there has been no one who has not previously [28.301] been a son or a daughter of ours. But
dhpak2.3:8.5: these two have grievously offended against us, and it is out of the question for them to stand in our sight. Let these
dhpak2.3:8.6: two take as much money as they need and go and live in some pleasant place. However, let them send the children here.”
dhpak2.3:8.7: So the two took the money which was sent to them, and giving their children into the hands of the messengers who came,
dhpak2.3:8.8: sent them to their grandparents. Thus it happened that the children were brought up in the home of their grandparents.
dhpak2.3:9.1: Of the two children, Culla Panthaka was still very young. Mahā Panthaka, however, used to accompany his
dhpak2.3:9.2: grandfather to hear the One of Ten Strengths teach the Dhamma. And as the result of his frequent visits to the
dhpak2.3:9.3: Teacher, his heart inclined to go forth. Accordingly he said to his grandfather: “If you would give me your
dhpak2.3:9.4: permission, I should like to go forth.” {1.243} – “What say you, dear grandson? Your going forth would please me
dhpak2.3:9.5: more than the going forth of anyone else in the whole world. If you are able to do so, by all means go forth.”
dhpak2.3:10.1: Accordingly the grandfather took Mahā Panthaka to the Teacher, who said: “Householder, you have won a
dhpak2.3:10.2: boy?” – “Yes, venerable Sir, this is a grandson of mine who desires to go forth under you.” The Teacher
dhpak2.3:10.3: bade a certain bhikkhu on his rounds for alms to give him the going forth. The elder assigned to him as a
dhpak2.3:10.4: subject of meditation the first five of the constituent parts of the body, and then gave him the going
dhpak2.3:10.5: forth. The youth learned by heart a considerable portion of the word of the Buddha, and when he was old
dhpak2.3:10.6: enough took his higher ordination, and by diligently applying himself to meditation attained Arahatship.
dhpak2.3:11.1: As Mahā Panthaka passed his time in the enjoyment of the bliss of absorption, in the enjoyment of the bliss of
dhpak2.3:11.2: the fruition of the path, he thought to himself: “Assuredly it is in the power of Culla Panthaka to experience
dhpak2.3:11.3: this same bliss.” Therefore he went to the rich man his grandfather and said to him: “Rich man, if you will give
dhpak2.3:11.4: your kind permission, I should like to let Culla Panthaka go forth.” – “By all means give him the going forth,
dhpak2.3:11.5: venerable Sir.” We are told that the rich man was profoundly attached to the dispensation of the Buddha, and that
dhpak2.3:11.6: when asked: “Of which daughter of yours are these two children the sons?” he felt ashamed to say: “Of [28.302] my
dhpak2.3:11.7: daughter who ran away,” and that for these two reasons he was only too glad to give them permission to go forth.
dhpak2.3:12.1: So the Elder Mahā Panthaka gave his brother Culla Panthaka the going forth {1.244} and
dhpak2.3:12.2: established him in the moral precepts. But Culla Panthaka, once gone forth, proved a dullard.
dhpak2.3:13.1: Like a fragrant red lotus that blooms in the morning without losing its scent,
dhpak2.3:13.2: behold the Resplendent One shining forth, like the sun shines forth in the firmament.
dhpak2.3:14.1: In four months he was unable to learn by heart this single verse. It seems that, in the dispensation of the
dhpak2.3:14.2: Sambuddha Kassapa, he possessed great wisdom, but that, after entering the spiritual life, he ridiculed and made fun
dhpak2.3:14.3: of a certain bhikkhu who was a dullard, while the latter was trying to learn the sacred word; and that this
dhpak2.3:14.4: bhikkhu, embarrassed by the ridicule to which he was subjected, was unable either to learn the passage by heart or even
dhpak2.3:14.5: to repeat it. As the result of that act, Culla Panthaka was reborn as a dullard, and every sentence he learned
dhpak2.3:14.6: put the preceding sentence out of his mind; indeed four months passed while he was striving to learn this one verse.
dhpak2.3:15.1: Thereupon Mahā Panthaka said to his brother: “Culla Panthaka, it is not in your power to master
dhpak2.3:15.2: this dispensation. In four months you have not been able to learn a single verse. How can you ever
dhpak2.3:15.3: hope to reach the goal of the spiritual life? Go from here at once,” and he threw him out of the
dhpak2.3:15.4: monastery. But Culla Panthaka was sincerely attached to the dispensation of the Buddha, and the last
dhpak2.3:15.5: thing in the world he wished to do was to leave the Saṅgha and return to the life of a householder.
dhpak2.3:16.1: Now at that time Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking an abundant supply of garlands and of various kinds of perfumes,
dhpak2.3:16.2: went to his own mango-grove, rendered honor to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and then rising from his
dhpak2.3:16.3: seat and paying obeisance to the Teacher, approached Mahā Panthaka, who was distributor of meals, {1.245} and asked
dhpak2.3:16.4: him: “Venerable Sir, how many bhikkhus are living with the Teacher?” – “Five hundred.” – “Tomorrow, venerable
dhpak2.3:16.5: Sir, bring the five hundred bhikkhus presided over by the Buddha and take a meal in our house.” – “The bhikkhu
dhpak2.3:16.6: Culla Panthaka is a dullard and has made no progress in the Dhamma. I accept the invitation for all except him.”
dhpak2.3:17.1: When Culla Panthaka heard that, he thought to himself: “The [28.303] elder accepts an invitation for
dhpak2.3:17.2: all these bhikkhus, but in accepting it, deliberately leaves me out. Beyond a doubt my brother’s
dhpak2.3:17.3: affection for me is gone. Of what profit to me any longer is this dispensation? I will return to the life
dhpak2.3:17.4: of a householder and spend my days giving alms and doing other works of merit.” So on the following
dhpak2.3:17.5: day, very early in the morning, he set out with the intention of returning to the life of a householder.
dhpak2.3:18.1: Very early in the morning also the Teacher surveyed the world, and seeing this incident, preceded Culla Panthaka to
dhpak2.3:18.2: the gate and walked back and forth on the same road Culla Panthaka had taken. As Culla Panthaka came along, he saw
dhpak2.3:18.3: the Teacher, and approaching him, worshipped him. The Teacher said: “But, Culla Panthaka, where are you going at
dhpak2.3:18.4: this hour of the day?” – “Venerable Sir, my brother has thrown me out, and therefore I intend to return to the world.”
dhpak2.3:18.5: – “Culla Panthaka, it was at my hands that you received the going forth. Therefore when your brother expelled you,
dhpak2.3:18.6: why did you not come to me? Come now, what have you to do with the life of a householder? You shall remain with me.”
dhpak2.3:19.1: So saying, the Teacher stroked him on the head with his hand, the palm of which was marked with the wheel, and taking
dhpak2.3:19.2: him with him, went and seated him over against the Perfumed Chamber. And creating by psychic power a perfectly clean
dhpak2.3:19.3: cloth, he gave it to him, saying: “Culla Panthaka, remain right here, face towards the east, rub this cloth, and say
dhpak2.3:19.4: as you do so: ‘Removal of impurity! Removal of impurity!’” {1.246} Just then meal-time was announced, whereupon the
dhpak2.3:19.5: Teacher, accompanied by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to the house of Jīvaka and sat down on the seat prepared for him.
dhpak2.3:20.1: Culla Panthaka sat down, facing the sun, and rubbed the cloth, saying as he did so: “Removal of impurity! Removal of
dhpak2.3:20.2: impurity!” As he rubbed the piece of cloth, it became soiled. Thereupon he thought: “This piece of cloth was perfectly
dhpak2.3:20.3: clean before. But through this body of mine it has lost its original character and has become soiled. ‘Impermanent, indeed,
dhpak2.3:20.4: are all existing things!’” And grasping the thought of decay and death, he developed insight. The Teacher, knowing that
dhpak2.3:20.5: Culla Panthaka’s mind had attained insight, said: “Culla Panthaka, think not that only a piece of cloth has become
dhpak2.3:20.6: soiled with dust. Indeed within you are the dust of passion and other defilements; remove them.” And sending forth a radiant
dhpak2.3:20.7: image of himself, the Teacher, appearing to be sitting before him, as it were, pronounced the following verses: [28.304]
dhpak2.3:21.1: Passion is called dust, not particles of dirt, “dust” is a name for passion;
dhpak2.3:21.2: monastics, having abandoned this dust, live in the Dispensation of one free from dust.
dhpak2.3:22.1: Hatred is called dust, not particles of dirt, “dust” is a name for hatred;
dhpak2.3:22.2: monastics, having abandoned this dust, live in the Dispensation of one free from dust.
dhpak2.3:23.1: Delusion is called dust, not particles of dirt, “dust” is a name for delusion;
dhpak2.3:23.2: monastics, having abandoned this dust, live in the Dispensation of one free from dust. {1.247}
dhpak2.3:24.1: At the conclusion of the verses Culla Panthaka attained Arahatship,
dhpak2.3:24.2: together with the analytic knowledges, and knowledge of the Three Baskets.
dhpak2.3:25.1: It appears that in a previous state of existence he was a king. Once, while making a ceremonial circuit of
dhpak2.3:25.2: the city, with sweat pouring down his forehead, he wiped his forehead with a clean cloth, whereupon the
dhpak2.3:25.3: cloth became soiled. He thought: “By reason of this body of mine a cloth so clean as this has lost its former
dhpak2.3:25.4: character and become soiled. ‘Impermanent, indeed, are all existing things!’” Thus did he acquire the
dhpak2.3:25.5: concept of impermanence. In consequence of this, in a later existence, removal of impurity became his salvation.
dhpak2.3:26.1: Jīvaka Komārabhacca offered the water of donation to the One of Ten Strengths. The Teacher said, covering the bowl
dhpak2.3:26.2: with his hand: “Jīvaka, are there no bhikkhus in the monastery?” Mahā Panthaka replied: “No, venerable Sir, there are no
dhpak2.3:26.3: bhikkhus in the monastery.” The Teacher said: “But Jīvaka, there are!” – “Very well,” said Jīvaka, and he sent a man
dhpak2.3:26.4: to find out. He said: “Go to the monastery and find out whether or not there are any bhikkhus there.” At that moment
dhpak2.3:26.5: Culla Panthaka said to himself: “My brother says: ‘There are no bhikkhus in the monastery.’ I will show him that there
dhpak2.3:26.6: are bhikkhus in the monastery.” And forthwith he filled the whole mango-grove with bhikkhus. Some of them were making
dhpak2.3:26.7: robes, others were dyeing robes, others were repeating the sacred texts. Thus did Culla Panthaka create by
dhpak2.3:26.8: supernatural power a thousand bhikkhus, each different from every other. So when Jīvaka’s messenger saw the numerous bhikkhus,
dhpak2.3:26.9: he returned and told Jīvaka: “Noble sir, the entire mango-grove is full of bhikkhus.” And right there the Elder {1.248}
dhpak2.3:27.1: Panthaka, having multiplied himself a thousand-fold, sat in the
dhpak2.3:27.2: charming mango-grove, until such time as he was called. [28.305]
dhpak2.3:28.1: The Teacher said to the man: “Go to the monastery and say: ‘The Teacher summons Culla Panthaka.’” The man went and
dhpak2.3:28.2: said what he was told to say. Thereupon the cry went up from a thousand throats: “I am Culla Panthaka! I am Culla
dhpak2.3:28.3: Panthaka!” The man returned and said: “Venerable Sir, they all say they are Culla Panthaka.” The Teacher said: “Well
dhpak2.3:28.4: then, go and take by the hand the first man that says: ‘I am Culla Panthaka,’ and the rest will disappear.” The man
dhpak2.3:28.5: did so. Immediately the thousand bhikkhus disappeared. The Elder Culla Panthaka returned with the man who came for him.
dhpak2.3:29.1: At the end of the meal the Teacher addressed Jīvaka: “Jīvaka, take Culla Panthaka’s bowl, and he will
dhpak2.3:29.2: pronounce the words of thanksgiving for you.” Jīvaka took his bowl. The Elder Culla Panthaka, like a young lion
dhpak2.3:29.3: roaring a lion’s roar, pronounced the words of thanksgiving, ranging through the whole of the Three Baskets.
dhpak2.3:29.4: The Teacher arose from his seat, and surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to the monastery. After the
dhpak2.3:29.5: bhikkhus had shown the Teacher the customary attentions, the Teacher, facing the Perfumed Chamber,
dhpak2.3:29.6: admonished the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the admonition of the Happy One, assigned a subject of meditation, dismissed
dhpak2.3:29.7: the Saṅgha of monastics, and then, having entered the Perfumed Chamber, lay down lion-like on his right side.
dhpak2.3:30.1: Now at eventide the monastics assembled from all quarters, and drawing as it were curtains of crimson
dhpak2.3:30.2: blankets, {1.249} sat down and began to praise the virtues of the Teacher. “Friends, Mahā Panthaka, not understanding
dhpak2.3:30.3: the disposition of Culla Panthaka, thinking merely: ‘In four months this dullard has not been able to learn a
dhpak2.3:30.4: single verse,’ expelled him from the monastery. But the Sambuddha, because he is unsurpassed king of the Dhamma,
dhpak2.3:30.5: within the space of a single meal bestowed Arahatship upon him, and together with Arahatship the analytic
dhpak2.3:30.6: knowledges, and with the analytic knowledges mastery of the Three Baskets. Oh, great is the power of the Buddhas!”
dhpak2.3:31.1: Now the Fortunate One, knowing that they were discussing this matter in the Dhamma Hall, thought to
dhpak2.3:31.2: himself: “It is my duty to go to them this very moment.” Accordingly he arose from the seat of the Buddha, put
dhpak2.3:31.3: on his gloriously dyed under and upper robes, girded himself as with lightning, and over his shoulders,
dhpak2.3:31.4: like a crimson blanket, threw the great robe of the Happy One. And coming forth from his richly fragrant
dhpak2.3:31.5: Perfumed Chamber, and walking with the stride of a noble elephant in rut, with the incomparable grace of
dhpak2.3:31.6: a [28.306] Buddha, he proceeded to the Dhamma Hall. And mounting the gloriously arrayed sublime seat of
dhpak2.3:31.7: the Buddha, and diffusing from his body the six-colored rays of a Buddha, even as the sun, newly risen on
dhpak2.3:31.8: the top of Mount Yugandhara, agitates the inmost depths of the sea, he sat down in the center of the seat.
dhpak2.3:32.1: Now the moment the Sambuddha arrived, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus ceased their talk, and became silent. The Teacher
dhpak2.3:32.2: surveyed the assembly with a soft, kind heart {1.250} and said: “This assembly is exceedingly beautiful. Not a
dhpak2.3:32.3: single hand is out of place, not a single foot is out of place; not a cough is to be heard, not a sneeze is to
dhpak2.3:32.4: be heard; all these bhikkhus, reverent with reverence for the Buddha, subdued by the majesty of the Buddha,
dhpak2.3:32.5: though I were to sit here for an aeon and not speak, would refrain from speaking first, would not so much as open
dhpak2.3:32.6: their lips. I alone have the right to decide when it is proper to begin to speak. Therefore will I speak first.”
dhpak2.3:33.1: Accordingly with sweet voice, a voice like that of Great Brahma, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, what is
dhpak2.3:33.2: the subject of your conversation now, as you sit here all gathered together? What was the subject of the
dhpak2.3:33.3: discussion which you so suddenly broke off?” When they told him, he said: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first time
dhpak2.3:33.4: Culla Panthaka has proved a dullard. In a previous state of existence also he was a dullard. This is not the first
dhpak2.3:33.5: time I have been his refuge. In a previous state of existence also I was his refuge. But in a previous state
dhpak2.3:33.6: of existence I made him master of the wealth of this world. Just now I made him master of wealth that transcends
dhpak2.3:33.7: this world.” The bhikkhus desired to hear all about it. Responding to their requests, he related the following
dhpak2.3:34.1: Once upon a time a certain young man who lived in the city of Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā for the purpose of
dhpak2.3:34.2: acquiring the arts and became the pupil of a world-renowned teacher. He was by all odds the most helpful to the
dhpak2.3:34.3: teacher of all the five hundred young men who were his pupils. All of his duties, such as attending to his feet, he
dhpak2.3:34.4: performed most faithfully. But he was such a dullard that he was not able to learn a single thing. The teacher
dhpak2.3:34.5: thought: “This young man is most helpful to me; I will instruct him in the arts.” But in spite of his best
dhpak2.3:34.6: efforts he was unable to teach him a single [28.307] thing. {1.251} When, after a long residence, the young man was
dhpak2.3:34.7: unable to learn a single verse, he became discouraged, and resolving to return home, asked leave of the teacher.
dhpak2.3:35.1: The teacher thought to himself: “This young man is a devoted servitor of mine. I should like to make a learned man of
dhpak2.3:35.2: him, but this I cannot do. However, I ought certainly to make him some return for the assistance he has rendered me.
dhpak2.3:35.3: I will compose a certain mantra for him and give it to him.” So he took him to the forest and composed for him the
dhpak2.3:35.4: mantra: “You’re rubbing! You’re rubbing! Why are you rubbing? I know, I know too!” And this charm he taught him, causing
dhpak2.3:35.5: him to repeat it many hundred times. “Do you know it now?” asked the teacher. “Yes,” replied the young man; “I know
dhpak2.3:35.6: it now.” Thought the teacher: “If a dullard by dint of hard labor once learns by heart a form of words, it will never
dhpak2.3:35.7: leave him.” And giving him money to defray the expenses of his journey, he dismissed him, saying: “Now go make your
dhpak2.3:35.8: living by this mantra. But in order that you may not forget it, keep repeating it over and over.” When he arrived at
dhpak2.3:35.9: Bārāṇasī, his mother said to herself: “My son has returned after acquiring the arts,” and held high festival in his honor.
dhpak2.3:36.1: It happened just at this time that the king of Bārāṇasī made a careful examination of his bodily deeds and the
dhpak2.3:36.2: like for the purpose of discovering whether he had been guilty of any fault. So far as he could see, he had been
dhpak2.3:36.3: guilty of no impropriety. But he reflected: “A person never sees his own faults; it takes other persons to see
dhpak2.3:36.4: them. I will make a tour of the city and listen to what others say about me. When people have eaten supper and have
dhpak2.3:36.5: sat down, they gossip and talk about all sorts of things. If I am ruling unjustly, they will say: ‘We are utterly
dhpak2.3:36.6: ruined by the punishments, taxes, and other oppressions of our wicked king.’ If, on the other hand, I am ruling
dhpak2.3:36.7: justly, {1.252} they will comment on my good qualities, paying me many compliments and saying: ‘Long life to our
dhpak2.3:36.8: king!’” So at nightfall he put on a disguise and went about the city, walking close to the walls of their houses.
dhpak2.3:37.1: At that moment some tunnel-thieves began to dig a tunnel between two houses in order to enter two houses by the
dhpak2.3:37.2: same tunnel. The king saw them and took his stand in the shadow of the house. Now in this house lived the young man
dhpak2.3:37.3: who had just returned from Takkasilā with the mantra. When the thieves had dug the tunnel, they entered the house
dhpak2.3:37.4: and began to look over the goods in the house. Just then the young man woke up and began to repeat his mantra:
dhpak2.3:37.5: “You’re [28.308] rubbing! You’re rubbing! Why are you rubbing? I know, I know too!” When the thieves heard this, they
dhpak2.3:37.6: exclaimed: “This man knows what we are up to. Now he will kill us.” And forthwith, dropping even the clothes they
dhpak2.3:37.7: had on, they fled in terror in the first direction that was handy. The king, seeing them fleeing and hearing the
dhpak2.3:37.8: words of the young man as he repeated his mantra, continued his tour of the city and then entered the royal residence.
dhpak2.3:38.1: When the night grew bright and the dawn came, the king summoned a certain man and said to him: “My man, go into
dhpak2.3:38.2: such and such a street, and in a certain house, where a tunnel has been dug, you will find a young man who has just
dhpak2.3:38.3: returned from Takkasilā after learning the various arts. Bring him to me.” The man went and said to the young man:
dhpak2.3:38.4: “The king summons you,” and conducted him to the king. The king said to him: “Friend, are you the young man that has
dhpak2.3:38.5: just returned from Takkasilā after learning the various arts?” – “Yes, your majesty.” – “Give us this mantra also.” –
dhpak2.3:38.6: “Very well, your majesty. Sit down on the same seat with me and learn it.” The king sat down on the same seat with
dhpak2.3:38.7: him, learned the mantra, {1.253} and then said to him: “Here is your fee as teacher,” and gave him a thousand coins.
dhpak2.3:39.1: Just at this time the commander-in-chief of the army said to the king’s barber: “When do you expect to shave
dhpak2.3:39.2: the king’s beard?” – “Tomorrow or the day after.” The commander-in-chief of the army gave the king’s barber
dhpak2.3:39.3: a thousand coins and said to him: “I have something for you to do.” – “What is it, master?” – “Go through
dhpak2.3:39.4: the form of shaving the king’s beard, but grind your razor very sharp and cut his windpipe. Then you shall be
dhpak2.3:39.5: commander-in-chief of the army and I shall be king.” – “Very well,” said the barber, agreeing to the bargain.
dhpak2.3:40.1: When the day came for the barber to shave the king’s beard, he moistened the king’s beard with scented
dhpak2.3:40.2: water, sharpened his razor, and held it at the king’s forehead. Discovering that the razor was slightly
dhpak2.3:40.3: dull, and realizing that he must cut the king’s windpipe with a single stroke, he stepped aside and
dhpak2.3:40.4: began to sharpen his razor again. At that moment the king remembered his mantra and began to repeat it,
dhpak2.3:40.5: saying: “You’re rubbing! You’re rubbing! Why are you rubbing? I know, I know too!” Beads of sweat stood
dhpak2.3:40.6: out on the forehead of the barber. “The king knows all about this business,” he thought. He flung his
dhpak2.3:40.7: razor to the ground in terror and prostrated himself on his breast before the feet of the king. [28.309]
dhpak2.3:41.1: Now kings know a thing or two; and the king of Bārāṇasī immediately said to the barber:
dhpak2.3:41.2: “Scoundrel of a barber, you thought to yourself: ‘The king doesn’t know about this.’” – “Spare my life,
dhpak2.3:41.3: your majesty.” – “Very well, fear not. Tell me about it.” – “Your majesty, the commander-in-chief
dhpak2.3:41.4: of the army gave me a thousand coins, saying to me: ‘Go through the form of shaving the king’s
dhpak2.3:41.5: beard, but cut his windpipe. Then I shall be king and you shall be commander-in-chief of the army.’”
dhpak2.3:42.1: The king thought to himself: “It is due to my teacher that my life was spared.” {1.254} He sent for the
dhpak2.3:42.2: commander-in-chief of the army and said to him: “Well, commander-in-chief, what is there that you have not received from me?
dhpak2.3:42.3: Henceforth I can endure to look upon you no longer. Depart from my kingdom.” With these words he banished him from the kingdom.
dhpak2.3:43.1: Then he sent for the young man who had been his teacher and said to him: “Teacher, it is due to you that my life
dhpak2.3:43.2: was spared.” And when he had so said, he bestowed high honor upon him and made him commander-in-chief of his army.
dhpak2.3:44.1: “At that time,” said the Teacher, “the young man was Culla
dhpak2.3:44.2: Panthaka, and the world-renowned teacher was the Teacher himself.”
dhpak2.3:45.1: Therefore when the Teacher had finished this Story of the Past, he said: “Bhikkhus, thus
dhpak2.3:45.2: in a previous state of existence also Culla Panthaka was a dullard, and at that time
dhpak2.3:45.3: also I became his refuge and established him in the possession of the wealth of this world.”
dhpak2.3:46.1: Again one day the bhikkhus began a discussion: “The Teacher indeed became a refuge to Culla
dhpak2.3:46.2: Panthaka.” Thereupon the Teacher related the Story of the Past found in the Cullaseṭṭhi Birth Story.
dhpak2.3:47.1: Even with a little capital, an intelligent and skilled person raises himself up, like a small fire blown into flame.
dhpak2.3:48.1: Having pronounced this verse, the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first time I have been a refuge to Culla
dhpak2.3:48.2: Panthaka; in a previous state of existence also I was a refuge to him. But in a previous state of existence I made him
dhpak2.3:48.3: master of the wealth of this world; just now I made him master of wealth that transcends the world. At that time the young
dhpak2.3:48.4: pupil was Culla Panthaka and the young merchant was I myself.” Thus did he identify the characters in the Birth Story.
dhpak2.3:49.1: Again one day in the Dhamma Hall the bhikkhus began a discussion: [28.310] “Friends, in four months Culla
dhpak2.3:49.2: Panthaka was unable to learn by heart a verse of four lines; but because he never relaxed the powers of his will,
dhpak2.3:49.3: {1.255} he became established in Arahatship and has just now become master of wealth that transcends this world.”
dhpak2.3:50.1: The Teacher came in and asked: “Bhikkhus, what is it that you are sitting here now talking about?”
dhpak2.3:50.2: When they told him, he said: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who arouses energy in my dispensation surely
dhpak2.3:50.3: becomes master of the Dhamma that transcends this world.” So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak2.3:51.1: Through activity, heedfulness, through self-control and through
dhpak2.3:51.2: restraint, the sage should make an island that no flood waters can overcome.
dhpak2.3:53.1: At the conclusion of the verse many became Stream-enterers and so
dhpak2.3:53.2: on. Thus, benefit arose to those who had assembled from the teaching.
